items.title: Ukraine reconstruction costs hit $588B as war marks four years

featured_image.name: Russia hits power stations after Ukraine counter-offensive

items.description:
As Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine enters its fifth year on February 24, 2026, UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the war "a stain on our collective consciousness" and renewed his demand for "an immediate, full and unconditional ceasefire" as a first step toward lasting peace. In remarks to the Human Rights Council on Monday, Guterres noted that more than 15,000 civilians have been killed and declared: "It is more than past time to end the bloodshed".[1][2][3][4]

The anniversary comes days after the latest round of US-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine ended without a breakthrough in Geneva, where negotiations on territorial control and security guarantees remain at an impasse.[5][6]

items.title: Russian oil exports top prewar levels despite four years of sanctions

featured_image.name: Russia's crude exports slump to the lowest in 11 months

items.description:
Four years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the volume of Russian crude oil being shipped abroad remains above prewar levels, even as the revenue Moscow earns from those barrels has fallen sharply, according to new data published on the fourth anniversary of the conflict.

The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, a Finland-based think tank known as CREA, reported on Tuesday that Russian crude oil export volumes in the 12 months ending February 24, 2026, remained six percent above pre-invasion levels, totaling 215 million tonnes. Yet revenues from those crude exports dropped 18 percent year-on-year to 85.5 billion euros, as Russia has been forced to sell at steep discounts to attract buyers. Total fossil fuel export revenues fell to an estimated 193 billion euros for the period, down 27 percent from comparable pre-invasion levels.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: EU leaders visit Kyiv as Ukraine marks four years of war

featured_image.name: Ukraine marks four years since Russian invasion - Yahoo

items.description:
On Tuesday, February 24, 2026 — exactly four years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion — Ukraine entered a fifth year of fighting with no end in sight, as its people continue to endure daily bombardment, displacement, and an energy crisis that has left millions shivering through one of the harshest winters in recent memory.

Senior European Union leaders traveled to Kyiv to mark the occasion. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa attended an official memorial ceremony, visited energy infrastructure damaged by Russian missile strikes, and held a trilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The Coalition of the Willing, a group of 35 countries convened by British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and French President Emmanuel Macron, held a videoconference reaffirming support for Ukraine. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte participated in a separate ceremony at NATO headquarters in Brussels.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: 2026 is deadliest start to a year for Mediterranean migrants, UN says

featured_image.name: Migrant boat docks in Crete after dramatic rescue

items.description:
The United Nations' International Organization for Migration announced Monday that at least 606 migrants have died or gone missing in the Mediterranean Sea since the beginning of 2026, making it the deadliest start to a year since the agency began tracking such data in 2014.[1][2][3]

The grim milestone came as search operations continued off the Greek island of Crete, where a vessel carrying roughly 50 people capsized on Saturday approximately 20 nautical miles south of the port of Kali Limenes. Twenty people were rescued, including four minors, and the bodies of three men and one woman were recovered, according to the Associated Press. About 30 others remain unaccounted for.[4][1]

items.title: Slovakia cuts emergency power to Ukraine over oil dispute

featured_image.name: Slovakia threatens to cut electricity to Ukraine over Russian oil spat

items.description:
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico on Monday ordered the state-run Slovak Electricity Transmission System (SEPS) to suspend emergency electricity supplies to Ukraine, making good on a two-day ultimatum that expired after Kyiv did not restore oil flows through the Druzhba pipeline.

"As of today, if the Ukrainian side contacts Slovakia seeking help to stabilize the Ukrainian energy grid, such assistance will be denied," Fico said in a video posted to Facebook. He said the measure would be reversed "immediately after the resumption of oil transit to Slovakia" and warned that further "reciprocal measures" could follow, including reconsidering Slovakia's previously supportive stance on Ukraine's EU membership.[1][2][3]

items.title: Venezuela frees nearly 2,200 under new amnesty law

featured_image.name: Venezuela has released nearly 2,200 people under new amnesty ...

items.description:
Nearly 2,200 people have been released from Venezuelan jails since a new amnesty law took effect on Friday, lawmaker Jorge Arreaza announced on Monday. Arreaza, who leads the commission set up to monitor the law's implementation, disclosed the figure as emotional scenes of family reunions played out at facilities including El Rodeo prison east of Caracas.[1][2][3][4]

The releases mark a rapid escalation from the weekend, when National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez said 1,557 amnesty requests were being processed "immediately" and that "hundreds of releases" were already underway. The law, unanimously approved by Venezuela's ruling party-dominated National Assembly on February 19, offers amnesty for crimes linked to political protests and confrontations dating from 1999 to 2026.[5][6][7][8]

items.title: France bars US envoy Kushner from government access

featured_image.name: France to summon Ambassador Charles Kushner over U.S. ...

items.description:
France on Monday blocked US Ambassador Charles Kushner from direct access to government ministers after he failed to appear at a scheduled evening summons at the Quai d'Orsay, the headquarters of the Foreign Affairs Ministry. According to a source cited by AFP, Kushner sent a senior embassy official in his place, citing personal obligations.[1]

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot had called Kushner in to explain the Trump administration's remarks about the killing of Quentin Deranque, a 23-year-old far-right activist who died on February 14 from brain injuries sustained two days earlier during clashes between far-right and far-left groups in Lyon. In response to Kushner's absence, Barrot moved to curtail the ambassador's privileges, acting "in light of this apparent misunderstanding of the basic expectations of the mission of an ambassador, who has the honor of representing his country," according to the foreign ministry.[2][3][4][5]

items.title: Study finds proto-writing on Stone Age artifacts in Germany from 40,000 years ago

featured_image.name: Stone Age symbols may push back the earliest form of writing

items.description:
More than 40,000 years ago, early humans living in what is now southern Germany were carving structured sequences of symbols onto ivory tools and figurines — marks that a new study argues represent the earliest known precursors to writing, predating the emergence of proto-cuneiform script in Mesopotamia by more than 30,000 years.

The findings, set to be published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, come from a collaboration between linguist Christian Bentz at Saarland University and archaeologist Ewa Dutkiewicz at the Museum of Prehistory and Early History in Berlin. Using computational methods drawn from information theory and quantitative linguistics, the team analyzed more than 3,000 individual marks found on 260 Aurignacian-era artifacts unearthed in the Swabian Jura region of southwestern Germany.[1][2]

items.title: Anthropic says Chinese AI labs used 24,000 fake accounts to copy Claude

featured_image.name: Top AI firm alleges Chinese labs used 24K fake accounts to siphon US tech

items.description:
Anthropic alleged on Monday that three Chinese artificial intelligence companies — DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and MiniMax — used roughly 24,000 fraudulent accounts to extract capabilities from its Claude chatbot in a coordinated effort the company described as industrial-scale distillation, according to a blog post and a report first obtained by Fox News Digital.[1][2]

The three firms prompted Claude more than 16 million times, siphoning outputs to train and improve their own AI systems, Anthropic said. The scale of each company's activity varied: MiniMax accounted for more than 13 million interactions, Moonshot AI for more than 3.4 million, and DeepSeek for 150,000, according to The Wall Street Journal.[3]
